## In-Depth LinkedIn Optimization With Marketing Management Techniques

[[This paper applies marketing management techniques to my professional brand on LinkedIn, using Canadian logistics, and freight transportation in particular, as the market in which I want to be hired, so that the analysis of the industry and of its job requirements can guide the way I present my experience to the recruiters and operations managers who make hiring decisions in Metro Vancouver.]]
## Research and Analysis
## Target Industry: Canadian Logistics

[[This project examines logistics in Canada, with particular attention to freight transportation and to the digital services through which firms book and coordinate their shipments. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (2018) defines logistics as the planning, implementation, and control of the movement and storage of goods, services, and related information, a set of activities that in business practice connects suppliers, production sites, warehouses, carriers, and customers. Although freight transportation is central to that process, reliable distribution also depends on inventory control, on order processing, and on the exchange of accurate information among everyone involved in a shipment.]]

The industry is closely tied to the domestic economy and to international trade, as transportation and warehousing contributed CAD 96.5 billion, or 4.3% of national GDP, in 2024 (Transport Canada, 2025b). In that same year Canada’s international merchandise trade reached approximately CAD 1.55 trillion, of which, measured by value, road transportation carried 46%, marine transport 21.1%, air 11.6%, and rail 10.5%, so the first set of figures describes the output of the transportation and warehousing sector, whereas the second describes the value of the merchandise flows that the network moves.

Mordor Intelligence (2026) estimates that freight transportation accounted for 60.88% of the Canadian freight and logistics market in 2025, and that share, combined with the growing use of digital freight marketplaces, makes this field a reasonable starting point for examining employers and the qualifications they look for. Freightera, a Vancouver-based business-to- business platform on which shippers compare and book freight, offers a useful example of this type of service (Freightera, n.d.-a).
## Historical Market Performance, 2021–2025

Ken Research (n.d.) estimates that the market increased from USD 97 billion in 2021 to USD 112 billion in 2025, a cumulative gain of approximately 15.5%, and more than half of that USD 15 billion increase came in 2022 alone, since annual growth stayed below 3% from 2023 onward.

## 2021: Recovery Exposed Supply-chain Weaknesses

[[Freight demand recovered as commercial activity resumed after the initial COVID-19 restrictions, and Transport Canada (2022) documented higher port container traffic and more truck crossings than in 2020 as trade flows returned. The transportation network nevertheless remained vulnerable, because container scarcity, overseas shipping delays, wildfires, and severe flooding in British Columbia disrupted key routes, and end-to-end container transit from Shanghai to Toronto through West Coast ports averaged 34.5 days that year, well above the 25.9 days recorded for 2019 in Transport Canada’s historical series (Transport Canada, 2026).]]
## 2022: Strong Market Value, Persistent Congestion

[[In 2022 the market estimate rose to USD 105 billion, the strongest annual growth of the period (Ken Research, n.d.). Upheaval in world supply markets supported export demand for]] Canadian commodities, while imported goods continued to put pressure on terminals and inland connections (Transport Canada, 2023), and the average container journey from Shanghai to Toronto reached 39.9 days, the longest of the five years reviewed (Transport Canada, 2026). [[Because freight prices and capacity constraints contributed to the higher market value, that value should not be read as proof of better service or of larger physical volumes.]]
## 2023: Weaker Goods Demand and Labour Disruption

Growth slowed to 2.9% in 2023 as inflation, higher financing costs, and softer spending reduced demand for some imported and industrial goods (Ken Research, n.d.; Transport Canada, 2024). The July labour dispute at British Columbia ports was especially disruptive, since merchandise imports cleared through those ports fell 18.5% relative to June and exports departing them fell 23.0%, according to figures that Statistics Canada (2023) did not seasonally adjust, and although transit from Shanghai to Toronto improved to 35.0 days, part of that relief reflected the reduced congestion that came as demand eased (Transport Canada, 2026).
## 2024: Recovery Differed by Corridor

The market estimate reached USD 111 billion in 2024, an increase of 2.8% (Ken Research, n.d.), while freight volumes recovered in several transport modes with results that varied across Canadian gateways, as Transport Canada (2025a) reported higher container activity at major ports alongside continued interruptions from labour disputes and extreme weather. Online retail, for its part, remained a meaningful source of distribution demand, since Statistics Canada (2026a) measured CAD 73.7 billion in e-commerce operating revenue for 2024, a figure 9.0% above that of 2023.
## 2025: Trade Reorientation Reshaped Freight Flows

Although the market estimate edged up just 0.9% in 2025, to USD 112 billion (Ken Research, n.d.), the geography of freight changed considerably, as Transport Canada (2026) found that Canadian merchandise exports to the United States fell about 5% while exports to other markets climbed roughly 16%. Truck entries into Canada decreased by about 5% and U.S.- linked rail freight weakened, but marine gateways gained from overseas trade, with the Port of Vancouver handling a record 170.4 million metric tonnes, 8% more than in 2024, and with container transit from Shanghai to Toronto improving to 33.3 days, although it remained noticeably slower than in 2019 (Transport Canada, 2026).
## Interpretation of the Historical Trend

Over these five years, a rebound in demand first exceeded the practical capacity of parts of the network, after which shipping conditions normalized, freight activity weakened on some routes, and service reliability gradually improved, until by 2025 trade policy was changing the geography of freight demand, putting transborder trucking under pressure while ocean-oriented corridors gained business. [[For employers, this history makes shipment visibility, contingency planning, customer communication, and adaptable routing more valuable than a narrow focus on shipment growth alone.]]
## Current Market and Outlook, 2026–2031

[[Mordor Intelligence (2026) places the freight and logistics market at USD 111.66 billion in 2025 and USD 116.63 billion in 2026, and its forecast reaches USD 145.05 billion by 2031, which implies a compound annual growth rate of 4.45%.]]
## Figure 2
Projected Canadian Logistics Market Value, 2026–2031
Note. [[Data from Mordor Intelligence (2026); intermediate years follow the 4.45% compound annual growth rate implied by the forecast.]]

Conditions during 2026 help explain both the opportunity and the risk contained in that projection, since real GDP increased 0.8% in the second quarter, supported by exports, spending, and investment (Statistics Canada, 2026b), while the Bank of Canada (2026) projects 1.0% real GDP growth for the year and warns of persistent energy-price pressures and uncertainty over U.S. trade policy. [[Its October report also forecasts annual inflation of 2.9% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027, so higher fuel and input costs could compress the margins of road-freight operators even if the nominal value of logistics services continues to rise.]]

[[Online commerce is likely to sustain demand for fulfilment, warehousing, and parcel delivery, as Mordor Intelligence (2026) forecasts faster growth in courier, express, and parcel services than in the overall market, a projection consistent with the expansion of online retail]] documented by Statistics Canada (2026a). [[Trade diversification, in turn, supports port, rail, and intermodal services, particularly when exporters need alternatives to the established U.S.-focused corridors (Transport Canada, 2026).]]

[[Digital systems can help companies plan routes, track exceptions, and coordinate shipments, although their value depends on how well they are integrated into daily workflows and on the capabilities of the employees who use them, and freight marketplaces such as Freightera already show how shippers can compare carriers and manage documentation online (Freightera, n.d.-a). Environmental performance also remains material, considering that transport was responsible for approximately 22% of Canada’s greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, including both passenger and freight activity (Transport Canada, 2026), which means that fuel efficiency, network utilization, and lower-emission modes could become competitive considerations for logistics providers alongside price and service.]]

[[In light of these conditions, the outlook can be described as cautiously positive, because demand is expected to shift toward specialized, data-enabled services even though labour availability, energy costs, climate-related disruption, and North American trade conditions may affect the pace of growth.]]

## Competencies in Metro Vancouver Job Advertisements

[[To test that decision against the local market, I reviewed 10 advertisements in Vancouver, North Vancouver, Richmond, Surrey, and Burnaby, three of them published on LinkedIn and seven on employer, staffing-firm, or local job-board sites, of which six describe freight or logistics operations and four describe inventory or planning work. I counted each competency once per posting whenever it appeared as a requirement, an asset, or an explicit duty.]]

All 10 advertisements describe communication with customers, carriers, colleagues, or other stakeholders, nine mention Excel or Microsoft Office, and nine refer to solving problems or resolving exceptions, while eight include operational records and eight name an operating system such as ERP, TMS, WMS, or MRP. Inventory or stock control appears in seven postings, and shipment scheduling or tracking and reporting or analysis appear in six postings each, three of which (C, E, and J) require both, so the two counts only partly overlap, given that a shipment coordinator needs to keep freight visible, whereas an inventory coordinator is more likely to work with counts, discrepancies, and performance reports.

## Priority Target Audiences

[[My primary audience consists of recruiters hiring for logistics, road freight, and distribution in Metro Vancouver, whom I prioritized because they screen candidates across roles with similar titles but different requirements, because they can reach my profile through LinkedIn search and location filters (LinkedIn, n.d.-d), and because the local postings show employers such as DSV, Rolls Right, and Hecny Transportation Canada hiring for roles that match my experience.]] My secondary audience is formed by the operations managers who evaluate candidates for these roles and who, once a recruiter has shortlisted me, need to see evidence of the work itself.

[[The operations manager persona, on the other hand, is responsible for a freight or warehouse team and needs someone who can keep an order moving when a plan changes, which is why this reader looks for evidence of how I handled a handoff or a status update.]]
## Positioning Statement

[[I want to be known for freight coordination and inventory operations, with data analytics serving as a way to support those responsibilities, and while my experience at GLT and Garage gives me two examples of operational follow-through, my industrial engineering education and postgraduate study at Douglas College help explain why I am also interested in reporting, inventory accuracy, and process improvement.]]

[[In practical terms, I will lead with my freight and inventory experience, using the headline to identify that direction and the About and Experience sections to explain the work behind it, and whenever I include a tool or a performance claim, I will connect it to a specific role, project, or result that I am able to discuss.]]

[[Expressed as a formal positioning statement, my proposition reads as follows: for logistics recruiters and operations managers in Metro Vancouver, I am a logistics coordinator with an industrial engineering background who keeps freight and stock visible, because I have provided freight-status updates at GLT Logistics, coordinated stock movement and replenishment at Garage Clothing, and completed postgraduate studies in data analytics at Douglas College.]]
## Marketing Mix: The 4Ps of Personal Branding

[[I applied the four Ps to my LinkedIn strategy (Gomez Albrecht et al., 2023), in which Product describes the experience I offer, Price gives me a basis for discussing compensation, Place identifies where I will reach employers, and Promotion sets out how I will show my work and take part in conversations, with Table 8 summarizing the decision that resulted from each element.]]
## Product: The Professional Value Offered

[[My offer combines freight coordination at GLT Logistics, stockroom operations at Garage Clothing, and earlier work in purchasing, planning, and operational indicators, a combination whose advantage is practical, since it allows me to speak about the customer side of a shipment as well as about the internal work needed to process and replenish stock. I will support the profile with descriptions of those responsibilities and with a work sample that demonstrates my analytical skills.]]

## Place: LinkedIn

[[LinkedIn is the channel where I will present my work history and make it easier for people in logistics to find me, although I will also use employer career sites whenever an advertisement directs me there, bearing in mind that a focused title, an accurate location, and relevant skills help a recruiter assess fit (LinkedIn, n.d.-a, n.d.-d).]]

[[I will follow employers such as Freightera, Purolator, Rolls Right, and DSV to learn what roles they advertise and what topics their teams discuss, and I will review each posting before applying, especially when the role requires a specific transport mode, language, or operating system.]]
## Promotion: Evidence and Sustainable Values

[[I will use short posts and comments to show how I think about operational work, for example with one post that explains what a shipment update should include when an ETA changes and another that shows how I would check a discrepancy in an inventory count. In both cases I will draw on public data or on examples I am able to share and will answer the comments that raise a specific question (LinkedIn, n.d.-c).]]

The market research also provides a relevant sustainability topic, since Transport Canada (2026) reports that transportation accounted for about 22% of Canada’s greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 and Freightera (n.d.-b) describes options for lower-emission shipping, which would allow me to discuss how load consolidation or mode selection affects both service and emissions and to relate that question to my interest in planning.

## LinkedIn Profile Review

The market analysis gave me the criteria for reviewing my profile, namely that a recruiter should be able to recognize the role I am targeting and that an operations manager should be able to see how my experience relates to the work, so I began with LinkedIn’s guidance on completing a profile and then compared my existing wording with the skills and duties found in the local advertisements.
## Recommendations for a Logistics Profile

LinkedIn recommends a recognizable professional photo, a background image, an About section that explains the professional story, and Experience and Skills sections that reflect career goals (LinkedIn, n.d.-a). [[The photograph therefore needs clear lighting, a simple background, and a crop that keeps the face recognizable on a small screen, while the banner can use the space beside the portrait to identify the area of work, and both elements should be checked on a laptop as well as on a phone.]]

[[The headline should name the work I want to be found for and use terms that fit my experience, and since LinkedIn explains that people search is personalized and considers profile attributes and filters such as location (LinkedIn, n.d.-d), the language of the vacancies becomes a useful starting point for choosing those terms. In my case, “Logistics Coordinator,” “Freight Transportation,” and “Inventory Management” are more specific than “Logistics” on its own, so I would use the role in the headline, explain the work in About and Experience, and attach a small set of relevant skills to the entries where I used them.]]

[[The About section can connect my experience across jobs by explaining the work I have already done, what I can offer, and the roles I am looking for, whereas the Experience section is where I can be more specific about what I handled and who depended on the information, as in providing a status update, coordinating with a carrier or warehouse, or resolving an issue that affects a shipment. When I have a verified result I can add its scope and period, and when I only know the responsibility, describing it accurately is enough.]]

[[Skills and Featured serve different purposes, because a skill such as SAP ERP describes what I can use, while a work sample shows how I apply an analytical method. Since LinkedIn supports adding relevant work, education, skills, and media to the profile (LinkedIn, n.d.-a), I would use a college project or a clearly labelled practice dataset to illustrate inventory analysis, explaining the question, the information used, and the operational decision it supports.]]

[[My visible activity consists mainly of short congratulatory comments, which help me stay in touch with colleagues but tell a recruiter little about my logistics interests. Following LinkedIn’s suggestion to share relevant professional knowledge and start conversations (LinkedIn, n.d.-c), I would keep interacting with colleagues while adding comments that contribute a practical point, such as what information a dispatch team needs when an ETA changes, and I could also ask a former colleague or supervisor for a recommendation about specific work we did together.]]
## Profile Assessment With ChatGPT and Resume Worded

[[I used ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2026) to compare the text of my headline, About, Experience, and Skills sections with the duties in the local advertisements, asking it to identify which requirements my profile already supported, which were present but difficult to find, and which needed more evidence.
